newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-MONEY FOR ATHLETES IN "SHAMATEUR" DAYS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-MONEY FOR ATHLETES IN "SHAMATEUR" DAYS.

text.p: American Dwight Stones, top high jumper in the 1970s, has revealed how he used to haggle for money before attempting to break world records in the days before athletics went professional.

Stones, who broke the world record three times between 1973 and 1976, said he would often discuss the bonus he wanted with meeting directors before he would agree to the bar being raised to a world record height.
"I was not going to raise the bar to the world record if I was not paid a bonus for it," Stones said in a British radio programme to be broadcast later on Wednesday.
"I would negotiate with the meeting director while the crowd waited for them to raise the bar."

The BBC Radio programme, hosted by Britain's former middle-distance champion Steve Cram, detailed how banned payments had been made to athletes for decades before the sport went professional in the 1980s -- the so-called "shamateurism" of athletics.
Britain's former top hurdler Alan Pascoe explained how Stones was keen to see the cash before he jumped at a meeting in 1976.
"Dwight said he would attempt a world record but he wanted to see his money," Pascoe said.

"All they could get from the bank was old one pound ($1.68) notes and someone walked across with what looked like a brick in a paper bag to give him his 1,000 ($1,680) or 500 ($840) -- whatever it was he got for that particular competition."
In the programme Cram said he was offered his first cash after he raised his profile by making the Olympic final at the 1980 Moscow Games. The money was often handed over in brown envelopes.
"Payments happened but nobody every talked about it," Cram said.
Former athletes also revealed how payments were also made as long ago as the 1950s.

Chris Brasher, who acted as a pacemaker to help Roger Bannister break the four-minute mile in 1954 and won the Olympic 3,000 metres steeplechase gold in 1956, cited examples of other athletes taking payment.
But, contrary to earlier reports, there was no suggestion in the programme that Brasher himself had received money.
"I knew of six athletes in the whole of Britain who did get paid," he said.

"The highest amount I heard anybody get for one race was 150 pounds ($253)...Maybe an athlete might make 1,000 ($1,680) in a year. It was all back door money, brown envelopes, that sort of thing." ($ = 0.592 British Pounds)
